entry.title: How fstrim Can Silently Trigger SAP HANA HA Cluster Failovers - A Root Cause Analysis from the Field
entry.content:
Abstract

A large enterprise customer running SAP S/4HANA on a scale-out SAP HANA database experienced repeated, unexplained Pacemaker HA cluster failovers over a period of several months. Each failover caused a complete business outage affecting mission-critical operations. After an extensive investigation involving SAP, the cloud infrastructure provider, the OS vendor, and the customer's team, the root cause was traced to a seemingly innocuous Linux system utility: fstrim.

This article walks through the investigation process, the root cause mechanism, and the resolution — providing actionable guidance for SAP HANA administrators managing HA clusters on Linux.

1. System Landscape

The affected production landscape consisted of:

  • SAP S/4HANA supporting sales, eCommerce, warehousing, transportation, and finance
  • SAP HANA database in a scale-out configuration
  • SUSE Linux Enterprise Server (SLES) with Pacemaker HA cluster (SAPHanaTopology / SAPHana resource agents)
  • XFS file system on NVMe storage via device-mapper (dm)
  • Cloud-hosted infrastructure (IaaS)
  • Third-party endpoint security (real-time antivirus scanning)

2. Problem Description

Over a span of approximately three months, the production SAP HANA system experienced eight HA cluster failovers. Some required manual intervention to restore operations. Each incident disrupted the customer's entire SAP S/4HANA environment.

A critical observation emerged early in the investigation:

Nearly all failovers occurred during the same narrow time window each week — the early hours of Monday morning (UTC).

This highly regular pattern became the single most important clue in the investigation.

3. Investigation

3.1 Phase 1: Ruling Out Antivirus Software

Because the HANA database servers ran a third-party endpoint security agent with real-time file scanning enabled, the initial hypothesis was that antivirus activity could be interfering with HANA processes or Pacemaker operations.

Actions taken:

  • Reviewed the antivirus agent logs for scanning activity on SAP/HANA/Pacemaker directories
  • Added directory-level and process-level exclusions for /hana/shared/*, /usr/sap/*, and Pacemaker paths (per SAP Note 2808515)
  • Completely disabled real-time scanning on a Sunday evening as a controlled test

Result:

  • No failover occurred on Sunday night (when fstrim was not scheduled).
  • A failover still occurred on Monday morning — even with antivirus disabled.
  • Log analysis confirmed the antivirus agent was not scanning HANA-related directories during the Monday failover window.

Conclusion: The antivirus software was ruled out as the cause of the recurring weekly failovers. (Note: The antivirus agent was separately found to contribute to IPC-timeout-related failovers at other times — a distinct issue addressed in parallel.)

3.2 Phase 2: Discovering the fstrim Correlation

With antivirus eliminated, the team systematically reviewed all scheduled system activities running during the failover window. The breakthrough came from inspecting the OS systemd timer configuration and system message logs.

Key finding:

  • fstrim.timer: configured to run weekly on Monday
  • Window: midnight to 1:00 AM UTC (with ~100 second random delay)
  • Actual observed runtime on production: ~27-30 minutes
  • Actual observed runtime on non-production: ~2 minutes

The fstrim execution window overlapped precisely with every recorded failover event. On SLES, fstrim.timer is enabled by default and runs weekly.

Immediate mitigation: fstrim was disabled on the production system. From that point forward, no further failovers occurred. The system remained stable for the entire subsequent monitoring period.

  • systemctl stop fstrim.timer
  • systemctl disable fstrim.timer

3.3 Phase 3: Understanding the Root Cause Mechanism

Disabling fstrim resolved the symptom, but the team needed to understand the technical chain of events — why a storage maintenance utility could trigger a database HA failover.

3.3.1 Pacemaker Cluster Monitoring Basics

The SAP HANA Pacemaker resource agent (SAPHanaTopology) periodically executes monitoring commands — including hdbnsutil and Python scripts — to verify system replication status and database availability. The key parameters are:

  • 60-second timeout. Each monitoring command has a
  • If the command does not return within the timeout, the cluster retries.
  • After multiple consecutive timeouts, the cluster interprets the primary node as unresponsive and initiates a stop/failover action based on the resource agent configuration and replication state.

3.3.2 Detailed Failover Timeline

Reconstructing a representative failover event from trace files:

Table 1: Pacemaker HA Failover Event Timeline (representative incident)

Phase

Elapsed Time

Event

Evidence

Normal

T+0

Last successful Pacemaker monitor action (SAPHanaTopology completes in ~6s)

Pacemaker log: "end action monitor_clone with rc=0 (6s)"

Degraded

T+10s

Next monitor cycle begins; commands start taking abnormally long

hdbnsutil calls no longer returning within expected timeframe

Timeout Loop

T+10s to T+6min

Multiple hdbnsutil / Python calls fail the 60s timeout after repeated retries

Each call stuck in process initialization (chmod on trace files)

Demotion

T+6min

Pacemaker demotes the primary DB and issues HANA stop command

Cluster resource state transitions logged

Failover

T+~13min

DB stop completes (~7 min); cluster promotes secondary to primary

Takeover completed; system back online

3.3.3 strace Analysis: Pinpointing the Blocking Point

To identify exactly where the monitoring commands were getting stuck, manual hdbnsutil calls were executed during and outside the problem window, traced with strace.

Table 2: strace Comparison — hdbnsutil chmod Latency (Normal vs. During fstrim)

Scenario

Command Traced

chmod Duration

Total hdbnsutil Runtime

Observation

Normal period
(outside fstrim window)

chmod("/usr/sap/<SID>/.../trace/nameserver_*.trc", 0640)

0.000012s (~12 μs)

~8 seconds

File metadata operation completes instantly; process initialization is trivial

During fstrim
(within issue window)

chmod("/usr/sap/<SID>/.../trace/nameserver_*.trc", 0640)

293.055634s (~4.9 min)

~5 minutes

OS file metadata operation completely blocked by storage I/O saturation from fstrim

The critical insight: hdbnsutil's actual database command executes in milliseconds. The time is spent entirely in process initialization — trace file setup, environment configuration — which depends on OS-level file operations (chmod, write, open). These OS operations were blocked because the underlying storage was saturated by fstrim.

Process state captures taken during the fstrim window confirmed the I/O blocking:

Table 3: Process State Capture During fstrim Window (ps output summary)

Process

State

Description

hdbnsutil (Pacemaker-initiated)

D

Uninterruptible sleep — blocked in kernel waiting for I/O on /usr/sap/...

hdbnsutil (manually initiated)

D

Same blocking behavior, confirming issue is OS-level, not Pacemaker-specific

backint (HANA backup process)

D

Log backup I/O also blocked; could not write to /usr/sap/.../backint/

fstrim

R / S

Actively running, issuing discard I/O requests against all mounted file systems

Endpoint security agent

S

Running but idle — real-time scanning already disabled at this point

Additional observations during the fstrim window:

  • HANA log backup operations stalled
  • Administrative SSH sessions hung
  • Even basic OS commands (ls, chmod) on affected file systems became unresponsive

3.3.4 OS Vendor Kernel-Level Analysis

The OS vendor's L3 engineering team analyzed the system core dump and provided a kernel-level explanation of the blocking mechanism:

// block/bio.c — submit_bio_wait()
// fstrim submits discard requests via this path and waits synchronously
int submit_bio_wait(struct bio *bio) {
    bio->bi_opf |= REQ_SYNC;
    submit_bio(bio);
    wait_for_completion_io(&done);  // <-- blocks here
}

The analysis revealed several compounding factors:

  • Severe free-space fragmentation: The XFS file system on the production volume had highly fragmented free space. fstrim with the default minimum block size had to process an enormous number of individual free extents, issuing a discard request for each one.
  • Discard storm: The flood of small discard I/O requests overwhelmed the storage path. Cloud storage backends, in particular, are sensitive to discard storms.
  • Block-layer throttling: The device had blk-throttle (I/O bandwidth throttling) configured. The kernel flag BIO_BPS_THROTTLED on the pending bio confirmed that discards were being rate-limited, further extending fstrim's runtime.
  • I/O path contention: The sustained discard I/O blocked other I/O requests sharing the same storage path — including metadata operations (chmod, write) on the /usr/sap file system where HANA traces and binaries reside.

# Key evidence from the core dump:
crash> dev -d | grep ff18ba9223888f20
  254 ff18ba905523d800   dm-3   ff18ba9223888f20   1   0   1
# NVMe disk backing dm-3 — the device where fstrim was issuing discards

# xfs_trim_extents called with start=0, end=2147475455
# processing the entire allocation group in a single sweep

4. Root Cause Summary

The complete chain of causation:

Step

What Happens

Technical Detail

1

fstrim runs with default minimum block size

On a large production file system with severe free-space fragmentation, this generates thousands of small discard requests.

2

"Discard storm" + block-layer throttling

The flood of discards saturates the storage I/O path. blk-throttle rate-limits the requests, extending total runtime to 20-30 minutes.

3

OS-level file operations blocked

Any process needing file metadata operations (chmod, open, write) on the affected storage path enters D state (uninterruptible sleep), waiting for I/O.

4

hdbnsutil initialization hangs

The HANA utility's startup sequence includes trace file operations (chmod on /usr/sap/…/trace/). A chmod that normally takes microseconds now takes 293+ seconds.

5

Pacemaker monitoring commands time out

Multiple consecutive hdbnsutil calls fail the 60-second timeout. The cluster concludes the primary is unresponsive.

6

HA failover initiated

Pacemaker stops the primary database and promotes the secondary — causing a full business outage.

Why was non-production unaffected? On non-production systems, fstrim completed in approximately 2 minutes — well within the Pacemaker timeout window. The production system's larger disk size, higher data volume, more severe free-space fragmentation, and different storage configuration caused fstrim to run 15x longer.

5. Resolution

5.1 Immediate Mitigation

Disabling the fstrim systemd timer immediately stopped the recurring failovers:

  • systemctl stop fstrim.timer
  • systemctl disable fstrim.timer

After disabling fstrim, the production system remained fully stable with zero unplanned failovers during the entire subsequent monitoring period (multiple months).

Storage snapshot sizes were monitored continuously after disabling fstrim. No significant growth was observed, confirming that disabling fstrim carried no adverse effects on storage efficiency for this environment.

5.2 Long-Term Recommendation

If fstrim needs to be re-enabled (for example, to optimize storage snapshot sizes), the key is to avoid the "discard storm" by specifying a larger minimum block size:

# Recommended: use a minimum discard extent size of 256KB or 1MB
fstrim -m 262144      # 256KB minimum
fstrim -m 1M          # 1MB minimum (skip small fragmented extents)

Testing on the DR system confirmed that fstrim -m 1M completed in ~126 seconds (vs. 20-30 minutes with the default setting), with /hana/shared accounting for ~111 seconds and all other file systems completing trivially.

Table 4: fstrim -m 1M Runtime Breakdown by File System (DR system test)

File System

Runtime with -m 1M

% of Total

Notes

/hana/shared

~111 seconds

~88%

Dominant contributor; large volume with mixed metadata

/hana/data

Trivial (< 1s)

< 1%

Minimal free-space fragmentation on data volume

/hana/log

Trivial (< 1s)

< 1%

Log volume largely sequential writes

/usr/sap

Trivial (< 1s)

< 1%

Small volume

Other FS

~14 seconds

~11%

OS and other mount points

TOTAL

~126 seconds

100%

vs. 20-30 minutes with default block size

When re-enabling fstrim:

  • Schedule it during a low-activity maintenance window
  • Monitor system with hdbnsutil and landscapeHostConfiguration running in parallel to confirm no blocking
  • Start with a monthly cadence rather than weekly
  • Use xfs_db -c 'freesp -s' to assess free-space fragmentation before and after

5.3 SAP HANA Does Not Require fstrim

From an SAP HANA perspective, there is no requirement to run fstrim. SAP HANA does not depend on or benefit from periodic TRIM/discard operations. The decision to run fstrim should be based on the OS and storage layer requirements of the specific infrastructure.

6. Lessons Learned and Recommendations

6.1 For SAP HANA HA Administrators

  1. Audit all scheduled OS-level tasks. Review systemd timers, cron jobs, and any infrastructure-level maintenance tasks that may run during HANA operation hours. Pay particular attention to I/O-intensive operations like fstrim, filesystem checks, and backup utilities.
  2. Be aware of default fstrim behavior. SLES enables fstrim.timer by default, running weekly. On large production file systems with fragmented free space, the default configuration can lead to extended runtimes that interfere with Pacemaker monitoring.
  3. Monitor OS-level I/O latency. Pacemaker monitoring commands depend on OS file operations. Any I/O blocking — from fstrim, antivirus scanning, backup operations, or storage-level throttling — can indirectly trigger failover. Tools like iostat and strace are essential for diagnosis.
  4. Leverage time-pattern analysis. Periodic failures almost always correspond to a periodic scheduled task. Correlating the exact recurrence pattern with system activity schedules is often the fastest path to root cause identification.
  5. Test fstrim behavior before enabling in production. Always run fstrim manually on a non-production system first, measure the runtime, and verify that it does not interfere with Pacemaker monitoring commands.

6.2 Investigation Methodology

The methodology that led to the root cause in this case can be summarized as follows:

Step

Approach

1. Pattern recognition

Identified the "every Monday morning" recurrence pattern

2. Elimination

Systematically ruled out antivirus, workload, and other suspects

3. Time correlation

Cross-referenced all scheduled tasks with the failover window

4. System-call tracing

Used strace to pinpoint the exact blocking syscall (chmod)

5. Kernel analysis

OS vendor L3 analyzed core dump to confirm I/O blocking mechanism

6. Verification

Disabling fstrim produced zero failovers over months of monitoring

7. Relevant SAP Notes and References

  • SAP Note 2808515 — Antivirus software exclusion recommendations for SAP on Linux
  • SAP Note 2578899 — Linux: kernel.pid_max configuration
  • SAP Note 2403162 — Impact of trace file flush activity on SAP HANA performance
  • SAP Note 3281130 — LNX: Server hangs at function call mutex_lock_slowpath
  • SAP Note 3665521 — Memory Reclaim of Huge Alignment Pages
  • SAP Note 3680406 — Optimizing Memory Allocation by Adjusting min_segment_size
  • SAP Note 2131662 — Transparent Huge Pages (THP) and SAP HANA
  • SUSE HA Extension for SAP HANA — Pacemaker resource agent documentation
  • Linux man page: fstrim(8) — discard unused blocks on a mounted filesystem

8. Conclusion

This case illustrates a fundamental principle of SAP HANA HA operations: any OS-level activity that can cause sustained I/O blocking is a potential trigger for cluster failover. fstrim, a standard Linux storage maintenance utility, became a "silent killer" under a specific combination of conditions — large file system, severe free-space fragmentation, block-layer I/O throttling, and cloud storage sensitivity to discard storms.

The challenge in diagnosing this issue lay in its cross-layer nature. It spanned SAP HANA trace initialization, Pacemaker resource agent behavior, Linux kernel I/O scheduling, XFS file system discard handling, device-mapper configuration, and cloud storage backend responsiveness. Resolving it required close collaboration among teams

entry.title: Planning Global HEX Enablement on SAP HANA - A Structured Validation Approach and Methodology
entry.content:
Abstract

A large S/4HANA system experienced performance regressions after globally enabling the HEX execution engine in a very earlier HANA release. The system-wide HEX setting was subsequently disabled and remained off for several years. With significant HEX fixes and improvements delivered in recent HANA versions, the decision was made to re-attempt global HEX enablement through a formal validation exercise.

This article focuses on three core topics: (1) how legacy query hints behave under the new engine, (2) a clarification of engine routing for legacy-interface queries, and (3) a 6-step validation methodology for global HEX enablement.

 

1. Background

1.1 HEX Engine Overview

SAP HANA Execution Engine (HEX) is the next-generation query execution engine on the SAP HANA platform. It leverages JIT compilation and operator fusion to improve analytical query performance. In recent HANA versions, HEX has become the default execution engine for most analytical queries.

1.2 System History

After an early attempt to globally enable HEX in this large S/4HANA system, several critical business workloads showed noticeable performance degradation. HEX was disabled at the global level. Over the following years, multiple rounds of selective testing were conducted, but each time certain query patterns — particularly those involving large financial tables, analytical reports, and BW queries — ran significantly slower under HEX than under the legacy engine. As a result, global HEX remained off.

 

 

Figure 1: HEX Engine Adoption Journey

1.3 Turning Point

With multiple core HEX issues fixed in later SPS revisions and the promise of broader HEX coverage in the newest release, the decision was made to proceed with a formal global HEX enablement validation on an updated HANA version (HANA 2.0 SPS08+).

  • Full Inheritance: The latest version includes all previous HEX fixes and performance improvements.
  • Progressive Enablement: Broader HEX coverage is provided; new features are disabled by default and can be activated via parameters.
  • Known Issues Cleared: As of the time of discussion, no known unfixed regression patterns exist.

 

2. Legacy Hint Behavior Under HEX

Long-running S/4HANA systems have accumulated many query optimization hints over time. When HEX becomes the default execution engine, these hints behave differently — some are ignored, some still take effect, and a few actively block HEX execution. Understanding these differences is an essential prerequisite before enabling HEX.

 

Figure 2: Legacy Hint Behavior Classification Under HEX (approximate distribution based on field experience)

2.1 Four Categories of Hint Behavior

Category

Behavior

Recommendation

Ignored by HEX
(Most legacy ESX/OLAP hints)

Query still executes on HEX;
hint has no effect

Can be kept; does not affect HEX.
Gradual cleanup recommended.

Blocks HEX Execution
(A few specific hints)

Forces the query to route
to the Legacy engine

Remove or replace with
HEX-compatible hints if HEX
is the target.

Shapes the HEX Plan
(Logical rewrite hints)

Still honored as optimizer
guidance; can alter the
operator graph structure

Keep and verify effect
using SQL Analyzer.

Independent of Engine
(Compilation/cache/script)

Does not affect HEX/Legacy
selection; only impacts
its own domain

No change needed.

 

Important: SAP has not published a formal compatibility matrix between hints and HEX. The classification above is based on field experience. Testing remains the only reliable method to confirm specific behavior.

 

3. Engine Routing for Legacy-Interface Queries

The system environment contains a significant number of queries executed through legacy internal interfaces (e.g., TREXviaDBSL). The initial understanding was that these queries are "hardwired" to use the OLAP engine and cannot benefit from HEX.

However, actual testing revealed that after removing certain hints, these queries could execute on the HEX engine. A more accurate explanation was provided:

Key Insight: Legacy interfaces support a SQL Mode — in this mode, the request is translated into a standard SQL plan and processed through the regular optimizer. HEX can then execute the generated SQL plan. Specific engine-routing hints force execution back to the OLAP engine. Therefore, OLAP routing is hint-driven (in SQL Mode), not an inherent HEX limitation.

This finding changed the hint cleanup strategy: for legacy-interface queries running in SQL Mode, removing the OLAP-forcing hint gives them the opportunity to benefit from HEX. However, each case must be tested individually.

 

 

4. Known Issue Resolution Across Versions

The HEX engine has made significant progress in stability and coverage from earlier versions to the latest. The following chart illustrates the resolution progress of key known issues across three major SPS versions:

 

Figure 3: HEX Known Issue Resolution Progress (SPS06 / SPS07 / SPS08)

Key improvement areas include:

  • Query Execution: Runtime optimization for complex predicate processing (e.g., multiple OR-concatenated LIKE conditions).
  • Correctness: Fixes for result correctness issues in specific index lookup scenarios.
  • Fallback Behavior: Runtime limits are now checked only during the first execution, reducing unnecessary fallbacks.
  • Diagnostics: Engine rejection reasons are now exposed in the SQL Plan Cache; Parameter Sensitive Optimization (PSO) is supported.

 

5. Global HEX Enablement Validation Methodology (6 Steps)

A 6-step validation methodology was designed and executed on a full production clone. The guiding principles are: establish a baseline, enable comparison, and ensure rollback capability.

 

Figure 4: Global HEX Enablement Validation — 6-Step Workflow

Step 1: Establish Baseline

Before enabling HEX, comprehensively capture the current workload performance baseline, covering runtime, resource consumption, plan cache state, execution engine distribution, and key business results.

Step 2: Global HEX ON Regression Test

Run representative workloads with global HEX enabled. Focus on high-cost SQL, CDS views, OLAP queries, large financial table operations, and ABAP-specific scenarios.

Step 3: Engine and Hint Impact Analysis

Check which statements actually use HEX, which still use Legacy, and whether existing hints affect engine selection. Use diagnostic tools to confirm hint effectiveness.

Step 4: Identify Regressions and Build Exception List

Build a structured exception list for statements showing performance regression, plan instability, or result inconsistency. Document impact scope and root cause direction.

Step 5: Validate Mitigation Actions

Validate mitigation options one at a time: clean up outdated hints, retain specific exceptions, adjust application logic, optimize data models. Keep before/after data and rollback options.

Step 6: Go / No-Go Recommendation

Synthesize all test results. Deliver passed workloads, performance improvements, regression list, parameter recommendations, and rollback procedures as the final enablement recommendation.

6. Regression Triage Checklist

When performance degradation is observed during validation, do not immediately attribute it to HEX. The following checklist helps teams systematically rule out other factors:

  1. Did the statement actually execute on HEX?
  2. Did the execution plan change?
  3. Did different parameter values cause different selectivity?
  4. Did the data volume change?
  5. Was the system workload or concurrency level different?
  6. Were there lock waits or resource blocking?
  7. Did recompilation or engine fallback occur?
  8. Did existing hints affect engine selection?
  9. Does the query pattern belong to a known sensitive scenario?
  10. Is it related to a known but unfixed issue?

 

7. Lessons Learned and Recommendations

  • Baseline first — Without comparison data, it is impossible to distinguish HEX regressions from other environmental factors.
  • Clean up hints before testing — Legacy hints can mask true HEX behavior or create false regression signals.
  • Test on a full production clone — HEX behavior is influenced by data distribution and volume; results from reduced test systems are not representative.
  • Earlier versions can be used for risk screening — If the target version is not yet available, the current version can be used for early screening, but final validation must be repeated on the target version.
  • Legacy-interface queries deserve a second look — Queries running through legacy interfaces in SQL Mode may benefit from HEX and should not be excluded wholesale.

 

References

  • SAP Note 2570371 - FAQ: SAP HANA Execution Engine (HEX)
  • SAP Note 2600030 - SAP HANA Parameter Recommendations
  • SAP Help Portal - SAP HANA SQL Plan Cache (M_SQL_PLAN_CACHE)
  • SAP Help Portal - SAP HANA Administration Guide

Conclusion

Globally enabling HEX is not a simple parameter toggle — for large systems that have had HEX disabled for years, it is closer to a structured technical validation project. The HEX engine has evolved from early instability to becoming the default execution engine, backed by substantial engineering effort from SAP to fix known issues and expand coverage. However, every workload is different, and a general "fixed" status cannot replace targeted validation testing.

entry.title: SAP HANA Stored Procedure to Update a Custom Field in VBPA Using VBAK-ERDAT After SLT Replication
entry.content:
Hi SAP Experts,

I have added a custom NVARCHAR(8) field to the VBPA table to store a date in YYYYMMDD format.

I need to develop a SAP HANA SQLScript stored procedure that performs the following:

  1. Identifies newly inserted records in VBPA through SAP SLT replication.

  2. Looks up the corresponding record in VBAK and fetches ERDAT.

  3. Updates the custom date field in VBPA with the fetched date.
